questions.stem: During a surgical procedure using electrocautery, a newer team member questions why the smoke evacuation system needs to run continuously when the surgical field already looks clear. The nurse should explain that this system is used primarily to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Reduce the overall equipment costs associated with the surgical procedure, which is not the actual reason for its use","B":"Speed up the pace at which the surgical procedure itself is completed, which is not the actual reason for its use","C":"Reduce staff exposure to surgical smoke, which can contain harmful chemicals and biological material even when the field appears visually clear","D":"Improve only the surgeon's visibility of the field, with no health-related benefit, despite the actual health-protective purpose of the system"}}
questions.rationale: Surgical smoke generated by electrocautery or lasers can contain harmful chemicals, particulates, and potentially biological material. Smoke evacuation systems are used to reduce staff exposure to these hazards, protecting the respiratory health of the surgical team.
questions.source_name: AORN — Surgical Smoke Safety Guideline
questions.source_detail: Purpose of Smoke Evacuation Systems

questions.stem: During a procedure using a surgical laser, a new team member puts on standard sunglasses instead of the eyewear provided at the door, assuming any dark lens will work. All personnel in the room, including the client, should instead wear:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Protective eyewear worn just when a person is directly facing toward the laser beam, rather than throughout the procedure","B":"Skipping eye protection entirely, contrary to what is actually required for everyone present during this kind of procedure","C":"Wavelength-specific protective eyewear appropriate for the particular laser being used, not standard sunglasses like the new team member put on","D":"Standard, non-specialized sunglasses, similar to what the new team member assumed would be sufficient"}}
questions.rationale: Laser procedures require wavelength-specific protective eyewear for all personnel in the room, including the client (when applicable), since standard eyewear (including regular sunglasses) does not provide adequate protection against the specific wavelength of the laser being used, and eye injury can occur even without direct exposure.
questions.source_name: AORN — Laser Safety Guideline
questions.source_detail: Wavelength-Specific Eye Protection Requirements

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing a client for an MRI scan, and the client mentions feeling completely calm and not at all anxious about the procedure. A critical safety screening step the nurse must still complete, regardless of the client's calm demeanor, is to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Screen the client and environment for any ferromagnetic objects or implanted devices that could pose a hazard in the strong magnetic field","B":"Skipping the screening process since the client appears calm and cooperative, reasoning anxious clients are the main concern to watch for","C":"Letting metal objects and jewelry stay on the client during the scan without any prior screening whatsoever taking place","D":"Assuming any implanted medical device the client might have is automatically considered safe for MRI without verification first"}}
questions.rationale: MRI safety screening is critical because the powerful magnetic field can cause ferromagnetic objects to become dangerous projectiles, and certain implanted devices (such as some pacemakers or aneurysm clips) may be unsafe or malfunction in the MRI environment. Thorough screening of the client, accompanying persons, and environment is essential before the scan.
questions.source_name: ACR (American College of Radiology) — MRI Safety Guidance
questions.source_detail: Ferromagnetic Object and Device Screening

questions.stem: A hospital implements a program to monitor staff hand hygiene compliance rates. This practice is an example of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A purely punitive measure implemented with no accompanying educational component","B":"An unnecessary use of hospital resources with no genuine patient safety benefit, since hand hygiene compliance is already assumed to be high","C":"A quality improvement strategy to identify gaps and improve adherence to a key infection prevention practice","D":"A monitoring practice that has no established relationship to actual patient outcomes"}}
questions.rationale: Hand hygiene compliance monitoring is a recognized quality improvement strategy that helps healthcare facilities identify gaps in adherence to this foundational infection prevention practice, guiding targeted education and interventions to improve compliance and, ultimately, patient safety.
questions.source_name: CDC / WHO — Hand Hygiene Compliance Monitoring Programs
questions.source_detail: Purpose of Compliance Monitoring

questions.stem: During a severe shortage of personal protective equipment, a facility implements "crisis capacity" PPE strategies, and a nurse assumes this means PPE is essentially optional now for certain routine tasks. The nurse should understand these strategies actually:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Eliminating the need for personal protective equipment during direct, hands-on client contact, contrary to what these strategies actually involve","B":"Representing the facility's preferred, standard approach to PPE use even when conventional supplies are fully available and plentiful","C":"Applying only to non-clinical support staff rather than to those providing direct client care, contrary to how these strategies actually apply","D":"Temporary, extraordinary measures like extended use or limited reuse of PPE, used only when conventional and contingency supplies are exhausted"}}
questions.rationale: Crisis capacity PPE strategies are temporary, extraordinary measures (such as extended use or limited reuse of certain PPE items) implemented only when conventional and contingency supplies are exhausted during a severe shortage, per CDC guidance, and are not the preferred standard approach under normal circumstances.
questions.source_name: CDC — Strategies for Optimizing PPE Supplies
questions.source_detail: Crisis Capacity Strategies During Shortages

questions.stem: During a mass casualty incident, triage tags are used to categorize victims. A victim tagged "red" typically indicates:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Immediate, life-threatening injuries requiring urgent intervention","B":"Minor injuries that can wait for care","C":"Deceased or expectant, with no immediate intervention planned","D":"Delayed but serious injuries that can wait a period of time"}}
questions.rationale: In standard disaster triage color-coding systems, "red" indicates immediate, life-threatening injuries requiring urgent intervention, while other colors (yellow for delayed, green for minor/walking wounded, and black for deceased/expectant) categorize victims by relative urgency of need.
questions.source_name: START Triage System / Disaster Medicine Standards
questions.source_detail: Red Tag Classification in Mass Casualty Triage

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing an isolation cart outside a client's room who requires contact precautions. The cart should be stocked with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"No specific supplies at all, since each staff member is expected to bring their own in this particular case","B":"Only surgical masks, regardless of the specific type of precaution required, since one type of mask is considered sufficient for any isolation type","C":"Gowns, gloves, and other PPE appropriate for the specific type of precautions required, along with signage indicating the precaution type","D":"Only a bottle of hand sanitizer, with no other protective supplies included on the prepared isolation cart"}}
questions.rationale: An isolation cart should be stocked with the appropriate PPE (gowns, gloves, and additional items as needed such as masks or eye protection) specific to the type of precautions required (contact, droplet, or airborne), along with clear signage, to support consistent and correct staff compliance.
questions.source_name: CDC — Isolation Precautions Supply and Signage Guidance
questions.source_detail: Appropriate Stocking of Isolation Carts

questions.stem: A client requiring airborne precautions is being placed in a room, and a newer staff member suggests any private room with the door closed will work just as well. The nurse should recognize the client should ideally be placed in a room with which special feature instead?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Negative pressure ventilation, which actively prevents contaminated air from flowing out into adjacent areas, unlike the plain private room the newer staff member suggested","B":"Standard room ventilation identical to what is used for any other hospitalized client currently on the unit at this particular time","C":"No specific ventilation requirements beyond the room's baseline airflow, similar to what the newer staff member had suggested earlier today","D":"Positive pressure ventilation, which would actually push contaminated air out into the adjacent areas rather than contain it properly in this scenario"}}
questions.rationale: Airborne infection isolation rooms (AIIRs) require negative pressure ventilation, which ensures that air flows into the room rather than out into adjacent hallways or areas, helping contain airborne pathogens and protect other clients and staff outside the room.
questions.source_name: CDC — Airborne Infection Isolation Room Requirements
questions.source_detail: Negative Pressure Ventilation for Airborne Precautions

questions.stem: A float pool nurse with a strong medical-surgical background is assigned to a specialty pediatric ICU unit outside their usual area of practice, and the charge nurse begins handing out full client assignments right away. Before this float nurse assumes a full client assignment, the facility should first ensure:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The float nurse being deliberately given the single most complex client assignment available on the pediatric ICU that particular day","B":"The nurse being expected to work entirely alone with no available resource support, given their strong general medical-surgical background","C":"No orientation or competency verification being required before assuming the assignment, given the nurse's overall years of experience","D":"The nurse's competency for this unit's patient population has actually been verified, with appropriate orientation and support first"}}
questions.rationale: Facilities have a responsibility to verify a float pool nurse's competency for the specific patient population and skills required on an unfamiliar unit, providing appropriate orientation and support, and typically avoiding assignment of the most complex clients to a nurse unfamiliar with that specialty.
questions.source_name: ANA — Principles for Nurse Staffing, Float Pool Considerations
questions.source_detail: Competency Verification for Float Staff

questions.stem: During a hospital's response to a large-scale disaster, staff operate under an Incident Command System (ICS), and a new staff member assumes this is just a temporary renaming of the usual chain of command with no real functional difference. This system is primarily designed to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Applying just to law enforcement agencies, with fairly little relevance to healthcare settings like the one currently responding here","B":"Eliminating the need for any organizational structure during the response, contrary to what ICS actually provides in this kind of event","C":"Permanently replacing the hospital's existing policies without exception, rather than serving its actual, more limited purpose in this kind of context","D":"Provide a standardized, scalable organizational structure for coordinating an effective emergency response, which is more than just a renaming of the usual chain of command"}}
questions.rationale: The Incident Command System (ICS) provides a standardized, scalable organizational structure used to coordinate personnel, resources, and communication during an emergency response, applicable across various settings including hospitals, to promote an effective, organized response to disasters or large-scale incidents.
questions.source_name: FEMA / Hospital Incident Command System (HICS) — Emergency Management Framework
questions.source_detail: Purpose of the Incident Command System

questions.stem: A nurse working in a telephone triage role uses standardized protocols to help callers determine the urgency of their symptoms, and a caller becomes frustrated, demanding the nurse just tell them exactly what condition they have. This practice actually requires the nurse to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Providing a definitive medical diagnosis to every caller over the phone, without much regard for symptom complexity, as this caller demands","B":"Use validated clinical decision-support protocols and sound clinical judgment to guide callers to the right level and timing of care","C":"Avoiding documentation of the call details in the client's medical record, since triage calls aren't considered part of the formal record","D":"Ignoring caller-reported symptoms and relying just on the written protocol without applying any actual clinical judgment"}}
questions.rationale: Telephone triage nursing practice involves using validated clinical decision-support protocols, combined with sound nursing clinical judgment, to help callers determine the appropriate level and timing of care needed (such as emergency care, urgent care, or self-care at home), along with thorough documentation of the encounter.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Ambulatory Care Nursing — Telephone Triage Practice Standards
questions.source_detail: Standards for Telephone Triage Nursing

questions.stem: A client expresses interest in obtaining a second medical opinion before proceeding with a major surgery. The nurse should:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Inform the client that seeking a second opinion is never permitted by the facility","B":"Actively discourage the client from pursuing a second medical opinion","C":"Support the client's right to seek a second opinion, which is a recognized patient right","D":"Assume the client is inappropriately questioning the current provider's competence"}}
questions.rationale: Seeking a second opinion is a recognized patient right, allowing individuals to gather additional information and perspectives before making significant healthcare decisions. The nurse should support and facilitate this process rather than discourage it, respecting client autonomy.
questions.source_name: Patient Bill of Rights — Right to Seek a Second Opinion
questions.source_detail: Nursing Support for Patient Autonomy in Seeking Second Opinions

questions.stem: A nurse is explaining the difference between a healthcare proxy (healthcare power of attorney) and a general power of attorney to a client's adult child, who assumes the two documents cover exactly the same authority. The nurse should clarify that a healthcare proxy specifically:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Grants the designated person authority over the client's financial affairs, with fairly little healthcare decision-making role involved","B":"Grants a designated person authority to make healthcare decisions for the client if they become unable to do so themselves","C":"Is identical in legal scope to a general, non-healthcare power of attorney covering just financial matters and transactions","D":"Has fairly little formal legal standing in healthcare decision-making, functioning just as an informal expression of preference"}}
questions.rationale: A healthcare proxy (or healthcare power of attorney) specifically grants a designated person the legal authority to make healthcare decisions on the client's behalf if they become incapacitated or otherwise unable to make decisions themselves, distinct from a general power of attorney, which may cover broader or different areas such as financial affairs.
questions.source_name: National POLST / Advance Care Planning Resources — Healthcare Proxy Definition
questions.source_detail: Scope of Healthcare Proxy Authority

questions.stem: A client has a Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) order in place, and a new nursing assistant asks whether this means the client should no longer receive pain medication or routine care. The nurse should clarify that this order specifically applies to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Withholding all forms of medical treatment, including pain management and routine nursing care, as the nursing assistant is currently assuming","B":"Preventing the client from receiving any form of ongoing nursing care whatsoever, including comfort measures, as the nursing assistant is currently assuming","C":"Withholding cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) specifically, in the event of cardiac or respiratory arrest, while all other appropriate care, including pain management, continues as usual","D":"Automatically applying to every future hospitalization with no need for reassessment at each new admission, contrary to how DNR orders actually need to be handled"}}
questions.rationale: A DNR order specifically addresses withholding cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in the event of cardiac or respiratory arrest. It does not mean withholding other appropriate medical treatment, comfort care, or routine nursing care, and the scope should be clearly understood by the entire care team.
questions.source_name: National POLST / AHA — DNR Order Scope and Clarification
questions.source_detail: Specific Scope of DNR Orders

questions.stem: A client with a significant cognitive impairment has a legally appointed guardian, but the client's adult sibling, who visits frequently, insists they should be the one making healthcare decisions instead. The nurse understands that healthcare decisions for this client should generally be directed to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The person holding formal legal authority for this decision, since that authority does not shift just because someone else visits often","B":"Any family member who happens to be present at the client's bedside at the time, such as the sibling currently insisting on this role","C":"No one, since a guardianship designation is mistakenly assumed here to have no bearing on healthcare decisions","D":"The client alone, with the appointed guardian having no role, based on the mistaken assumption that guardianship applies only to financial matters"}}
questions.rationale: When a client has a legally appointed guardian (established through a formal legal process due to incapacity), healthcare decisions are generally directed to the guardian, who has been granted legal authority to make decisions on the client's behalf, while still involving the client to the extent possible.
questions.source_name: Legal and Ethical Foundations of Nursing Practice — Guardianship
questions.source_detail: Role of Legal Guardian in Healthcare Decision-Making

questions.stem: A nurse manager is comparing typical nurse-to-patient staffing ratios between an intensive care unit (ICU) and a general medical-surgical unit. The nurse manager understands that ICU ratios are generally:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Lower (fewer patients per nurse) than medical-surgical units, reflecting the higher acuity and closer monitoring needs of critically ill clients","B":"A ratio that has no established relationship to client safety or clinical outcomes, since staffing levels are determined solely by budget","C":"A ratio that is identical to medical-surgical units across every single healthcare facility nationwide","D":"Higher, meaning more clients assigned to each nurse than on a medical-surgical unit, reflecting lower acuity needs"}}
questions.rationale: ICU nurse-to-patient ratios are generally lower (fewer patients assigned per nurse, such as 1:1 or 1:2) compared to general medical-surgical units, reflecting the higher acuity, complexity, and closer monitoring needs of critically ill clients in intensive care settings.
questions.source_name: ANA / AACN — Staffing Ratio Considerations by Unit Acuity
questions.source_detail: ICU vs. Medical-Surgical Staffing Ratio Differences

questions.stem: A client diagnosed with acute compartment syndrome is being prepared for treatment. The nurse should anticipate the need for:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Simple elevation of the affected limb alone, with no further intervention needed","B":"Emergency fasciotomy, a surgical procedure to relieve pressure within the affected compartment","C":"Oral pain medication alone, with no surgical intervention planned or anticipated","D":"Application of an additional, tighter cast or dressing over the affected limb"}}
questions.rationale: Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency requiring prompt fasciotomy — a surgical procedure that releases the fascia to relieve dangerously elevated pressure within the affected muscle compartment, preventing permanent tissue and nerve damage. Delaying treatment risks limb loss.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons — Acute Compartment Syndrome Treatment
questions.source_detail: Fasciotomy as Emergency Treatment

questions.stem: A client in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) has a serum potassium level of 3.0 mEq/L before insulin therapy begins. The nurse should anticipate that the provider will:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Start insulin therapy immediately, with no particular attention paid to the client's current serum potassium level","B":"Administer a potassium-wasting diuretic immediately, before starting insulin therapy, in order to further lower the serum potassium level","C":"Withhold all treatment entirely until the serum potassium level has fully normalized before ever starting the client's insulin therapy","D":"Address the low potassium level (often with potassium replacement) before or concurrently with starting insulin, since insulin therapy will further lower serum potassium"}}
questions.rationale: Insulin therapy drives potassium into cells, further lowering an already low serum potassium level, which can precipitate dangerous cardiac arrhythmias. When a client in DKA has hypokalemia, potassium replacement is typically addressed before or concurrently with starting insulin therapy, per standard DKA management protocols.
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association — DKA Management Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Potassium Management in DKA Treatment

questions.stem: A nurse is trying to distinguish between serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) in a client with altered mental status and elevated temperature. One key distinguishing feature is that serotonin syndrome typically presents with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Findings that are identical between the two conditions, with no distinguishing features at all in this particular clinical scenario overall","B":"Hyperreflexia and myoclonus, whereas NMS more typically presents with significant \"lead-pipe\" muscle rigidity","C":"An absence of any neuromuscular findings in either of these two conditions","D":"Hypothermia as the hallmark feature, whereas NMS is instead characterized by hyperthermia"}}
questions.rationale: While both conditions can present with altered mental status and hyperthermia, serotonin syndrome is more typically associated with hyperreflexia, myoclonus (muscle jerks), and gastrointestinal symptoms, whereas NMS is more classically associated with significant, uniform "lead-pipe" muscle rigidity and a more gradual onset, though clinical overlap can occur.
questions.source_name: Cleveland Clinic — Serotonin Syndrome vs. NMS Distinguishing Features
questions.source_detail: Key Clinical Differences Between the Two Syndromes

questions.stem: A client is treated successfully for anaphylaxis and symptoms resolve. The nurse should still recommend a period of observation because:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A biphasic reaction (recurrence of anaphylaxis symptoms) can occur hours after the initial resolution, even without re-exposure to the trigger","B":"The client can safely be discharged immediately with no further period of monitoring following the initial treatment","C":"A period of observation is never considered medically necessary after treated anaphylaxis in this particular clinical scenario overall","D":"No meaningful risk of the client's symptoms recurring after the initial treatment, since anaphylaxis is considered a single, self-limited event"}}
questions.rationale: A biphasic anaphylactic reaction, in which symptoms recur hours after apparent resolution of the initial episode (without re-exposure to the trigger), is a recognized phenomenon. A period of observation after treatment, along with clear instructions to seek care if symptoms recur, is recommended.
questions.source_name: World Allergy Organization — Anaphylaxis Guidance, Biphasic Reactions
questions.source_detail: Risk and Recognition of Biphasic Anaphylaxis

questions.stem: A client who was exercising outdoors in extreme heat presents with a body temperature of 40.5°C (105°F), confusion, and hot, dry skin. The nurse should recognize this as consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Simple dehydration alone, a condition that requires no urgent nursing intervention","B":"Heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate aggressive cooling","C":"Heat exhaustion, a milder heat-related condition requiring only oral fluid replacement","D":"A normal, expected physiologic response to strenuous outdoor exercise"}}
questions.rationale: Heat stroke is distinguished from the milder heat exhaustion by a significantly elevated core body temperature (often above 40°C/104°F) combined with central nervous system dysfunction (such as confusion), and often hot, dry skin (though sweating may still be present in exertional heat stroke). It is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate, aggressive cooling measures.
questions.source_name: CDC / American College of Sports Medicine — Heat-Related Illness Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Distinguishing Heat Stroke from Heat Exhaustion

questions.stem: A client found outdoors in cold weather has a core body temperature of 31°C (87.8°F) and is confused with slowed reflexes. The nurse should recognize this as consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Mild hypothermia, a milder classification than what this client's presentation reflects","B":"Heat exhaustion, a heat-related rather than cold-related condition, which would be an inconsistent diagnosis for this presentation","C":"Moderate hypothermia, requiring careful, gradual rewarming and close monitoring for cardiac complications","D":"A normal, expected core body temperature requiring no nursing intervention"}}
questions.rationale: Moderate hypothermia (generally defined as a core temperature roughly 28-32°C/82-90°F) presents with confusion, slowed reflexes, and increasing cardiovascular instability. Careful, typically gradual rewarming (to avoid complications like rewarming shock or arrhythmias) and close cardiac monitoring are essential in this range.
questions.source_name: Wilderness Medical Society — Hypothermia Management Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Staging and Management of Hypothermia

questions.stem: A client with frostbite of the fingers arrives at the emergency department, and a family member mentions they tried rubbing the fingers vigorously in the car on the way in to "get the blood flowing." The nurse should anticipate the appropriate rewarming method to instead be:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Rapid rewarming in warm (not hot) water, around 37-39°C (98.6-102°F), avoiding refreezing after rewarming begins","B":"Continued vigorous rubbing or massaging of the affected fingers, similar to what the family already tried in the car","C":"Rapid rewarming using dry heat, such as a heating pad or direct open flame, applied to the frostbitten tissue","D":"Slow, passive rewarming at room temperature over the course of several days rather than a rapid warm-water method"}}
questions.rationale: Standard frostbite treatment involves rapid rewarming in warm (not hot) water within a specific temperature range, avoiding dry heat sources (which risk burns) and vigorous rubbing (which can cause further tissue damage). It is critical to avoid any risk of refreezing once rewarming has begun, since this significantly worsens tissue damage.
questions.source_name: Wilderness Medical Society — Frostbite Management Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Proper Rewarming Technique for Frostbite

questions.stem: A client is rescued after a near-drowning incident and is breathing spontaneously and talking normally shortly after being pulled from the water, leading the family to ask about going home right away. The nurse should anticipate close monitoring for which delayed complication before considering discharge?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Immediate discharge home with no period of observation for delayed complications, as the family is currently hoping will happen very soon","B":"Delayed pulmonary complications, such as pulmonary edema, which can develop hours later even if breathing seems fine at first","C":"No further monitoring being needed once the client resumes spontaneous breathing, supporting the family's request to go home right now today","D":"An improvement in lung function that requires no ongoing monitoring at all after this kind of near-drowning event actually occurred earlier"}}
questions.rationale: Even clients who appear to recover well immediately after a near-drowning incident require close monitoring, since delayed pulmonary complications such as pulmonary edema (sometimes called "secondary drowning" or delayed-onset respiratory distress) can develop hours later, making an observation period essential.
questions.source_name: American Heart Association / Wilderness Medical Society — Drowning Management Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Risk of Delayed Pulmonary Complications After Near-Drowning

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client receiving a medication that requires therapeutic drug monitoring with peak and trough levels, and a new team member draws a random level partway through the infusion, unsure of the actual timing rules. The nurse understands that the "trough" level should actually be drawn:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"At the highest point of drug concentration, shortly after the medication is administered, rather than the timing the trough level actually requires","B":"At a random time unrelated to the client's actual dosing schedule, similar to what the new team member just did","C":"Immediately before the next scheduled dose, reflecting the lowest drug concentration, rather than the random timing the new team member used","D":"Only a single time overall, regardless of how many total doses have been given throughout the course of therapy"}}
questions.rationale: The trough level is drawn immediately before the next scheduled dose, reflecting the lowest point of drug concentration in that dosing interval, which helps assess whether the drug is being adequately cleared and whether accumulation or subtherapeutic levels are occurring.
questions.source_name: Clinical Pharmacology Reference — Therapeutic Drug Monitoring Principles
questions.source_detail: Definition and Timing of Trough Levels

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a client's electrolyte panel and notes an elevated anion gap in a client with a history of poorly controlled diabetes and a fruity odor to their breath. This finding, together with the client's presentation, is most commonly associated with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A finding generally considered a normal part of the client's baseline metabolic state, despite the abnormal value and concerning presentation","B":"Metabolic alkalosis specifically, a condition not typically associated with an elevated anion gap or this client's presentation","C":"Metabolic acidosis with excess unmeasured acids, such as in DKA, which fits both the elevated anion gap and this client's diabetes history and fruity breath odor","D":"A primary respiratory dysfunction with no associated metabolic component, despite the metabolic lab finding and presentation described"}}
questions.rationale: An elevated anion gap is commonly associated with metabolic acidosis caused by the accumulation of unmeasured acids, such as in diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, or certain toxic ingestions (e.g., methanol, ethylene glycol), helping guide further diagnostic evaluation of the underlying cause.
questions.source_name: Clinical Laboratory Reference Standards — Anion Gap Interpretation
questions.source_detail: Elevated Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis

questions.stem: A client found unresponsive at home is brought to the emergency department with dry mucous membranes, and labs reveal a serum osmolality significantly elevated above the normal range along with a glucose of 650 mg/dL. The nurse should recognize this elevated osmolality as most consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A state of overhydration, a condition generally associated with a low, rather than high, serum osmolality overall in most clients","B":"A hyperosmolar state, often associated with severe dehydration or significant hyperglycemia, consistent with this client's presentation and glucose level","C":"A normal laboratory finding requiring no further nursing assessment, despite the client's unresponsive state and abnormal glucose reading","D":"Hyponatremia exclusively, a finding generally associated with a low osmolality rather than the elevated value actually seen here"}}
questions.rationale: Normal serum osmolality is generally about 275-295 mOsm/kg. A significantly elevated value suggests a hyperosmolar state, which can occur with severe dehydration, significant hyperglycemia (as in hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state), or other conditions causing solute concentration in the blood.
questions.source_name: Clinical Laboratory Reference Standards — Serum Osmolality
questions.source_detail: Normal Range and Hyperosmolar State

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing INR targets for two different clients on warfarin: one with atrial fibrillation and one with a mechanical heart valve. The nurse understands that:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"INR targets are not used to guide anticoagulation therapy for either of these two clinical conditions, since dosing is based on weight alone","B":"The client with a mechanical heart valve typically requires a higher INR target range than the client with atrial fibrillation alone, due to greater thrombotic risk","C":"Both clients share an identical INR target range regardless of their specific diagnosis or thrombotic risk profile","D":"The client with atrial fibrillation requires a higher INR target than the client with a mechanical heart valve"}}
questions.rationale: While the standard INR target for atrial fibrillation is generally 2.0-3.0, clients with certain mechanical heart valves often require a higher target range (such as 2.5-3.5 or higher, depending on the valve type and position), reflecting the greater thrombotic risk associated with these prosthetic devices.
questions.source_name: ACC/AHA — Valvular Heart Disease and Anticoagulation Guidelines
questions.source_detail: INR Target Variation by Indication

questions.stem: A nurse notes that a client's BUN-to-creatinine ratio is significantly elevated, with a proportionally greater rise in BUN compared to creatinine. This pattern can suggest:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A normal finding with no clinical significance for the client's current condition in this particular clinical scenario overall","B":"A postrenal cause specifically, such as an obstruction within the urinary tract","C":"An improvement in the client's overall renal function and filtration capacity","D":"A prerenal cause of renal impairment, such as dehydration or reduced renal perfusion"}}
questions.rationale: A disproportionately elevated BUN relative to creatinine can suggest a prerenal cause of renal impairment (such as dehydration, reduced renal perfusion, or GI bleeding), since BUN is more sensitive to these factors than creatinine, helping guide further clinical evaluation.
questions.source_name: Clinical Laboratory Reference Standards — BUN/Creatinine Ratio Interpretation
questions.source_detail: Prerenal Pattern of Elevated BUN/Creatinine Ratio

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing hemodynamic monitoring data for a critically ill client whose cardiac output reads 2.1 liters per minute on the monitor, prompting the nurse to notify the provider immediately. The nurse understands that normal cardiac output for an average adult at rest is generally:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A value with no established normal range, making the nurse's concern about this particular reading unwarranted","B":"Less than 1 liter per minute, a range that would make this client's reading seem less concerning than it actually is","C":"Approximately 4-8 liters per minute, meaning this client's reading of 2.1 is significantly below normal and warrants the notification","D":"Roughly 20-30 liters per minute, a range well above what would actually be considered normal for this client"}}
questions.rationale: Normal cardiac output for an average adult at rest is generally about 4-8 liters per minute, though this varies based on body size and other factors. Cardiac output significantly below or above this range can indicate cardiovascular compromise requiring further assessment and intervention.
questions.source_name: Clinical Hemodynamic Monitoring References — Normal Cardiac Output
questions.source_detail: Normal Adult Cardiac Output Range

questions.stem: A nurse is suctioning a client's tracheostomy tube after noting coarse breath sounds and a drop in oxygen saturation to 89%. A newer colleague suggests just holding continuous suction the whole time to clear secretions faster. Correct technique instead includes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Applying suction only during withdrawal, using intermittent suction, and limiting each pass to a brief duration","B":"Suctioning for as long as necessary to fully clear the airway of secretions, with no set time limit placed on each individual pass","C":"Inserting the catheter as deep as possible while applying continuous suction throughout, similar to what the colleague had suggested","D":"Applying continuous suction during both insertion and withdrawal of the catheter, increasing the overall risk of mucosal tissue trauma"}}
questions.rationale: Correct tracheostomy suctioning technique involves inserting the catheter without suction, then applying intermittent suction only during withdrawal, limiting each pass to a brief duration (typically 10-15 seconds) to minimize hypoxia and mucosal trauma.
questions.source_name: AARC (American Association for Respiratory Care) — Tracheal Suctioning Clinical Practice Guideline
questions.source_detail: Proper Suctioning Technique

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client with a chest tube connected to a closed drainage system, and a nursing assistant offers to place the collection unit up on the client's bedside table for easier viewing. The nurse should ensure the collection unit instead remains:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Above the level of the client's chest at all times, similar to what the assistant just suggested, to promote gravity drainage","B":"Below the level of the client's chest, to allow proper gravity drainage and prevent backflow, rather than up on the bedside table","C":"Disconnected periodically from the collection system for the client's own comfort throughout the shift","D":"Clamped continuously throughout the day in order to prevent any air leaks from affecting the drainage system"}}
questions.rationale: The chest tube collection/drainage unit should be kept below the level of the client's chest at all times to allow proper gravity drainage of fluid/air and to prevent backflow of drainage into the pleural space, which could cause complications. Routine clamping is generally avoided unless specifically ordered.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Chest Tube Management
questions.source_detail: Proper Positioning of Chest Tube Drainage System

questions.stem: A nurse is providing routine care for a client with an indwelling urinary (Foley) catheter. Appropriate care includes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Disconnecting the catheter from the drainage bag frequently for the client's convenience","B":"Emptying the drainage bag only once per week regardless of the total volume of urine collected","C":"Keeping the drainage bag below the level of the bladder at all times and maintaining a closed, unobstructed system","D":"Allowing the tubing to loop upward above the level of the client's bladder, which can promote urine reflux and infection"}}
questions.rationale: Proper Foley catheter care includes keeping the drainage bag below the level of the bladder at all times (to prevent backflow and reduce CAUTI risk), maintaining a closed, unobstructed drainage system, and avoiding unnecessary disconnection, which increases infection risk.
questions.source_name: CDC — CAUTI Prevention: Foley Catheter Maintenance Care
questions.source_detail: Proper Positioning and Closed System Maintenance

questions.stem: A nurse is irrigating a client's sacral wound as part of routine wound care, and a student nurse asks whether the direction of irrigation actually matters. Correct technique generally involves irrigating:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Using unsterile tap water for irrigating this wound without a specific provider order permitting that approach","B":"From the most heavily contaminated area of the wound toward the least contaminated area, working outward, contrary to what is actually recommended","C":"With no particular attention paid to direction or a systematic technique, working from any area first, contrary to what the student is asking about","D":"From the least contaminated area toward the most contaminated area, such as from the wound center outward, answering the student's question directly"}}
questions.rationale: Standard wound irrigation technique generally involves irrigating from the least contaminated area toward the most contaminated area (such as from the wound itself outward, or working from a cleaner region toward a dirtier one), using an appropriate sterile solution as ordered, to avoid introducing additional contamination into the wound.
questions.source_name: Wound, Ostomy and Continence Nurses Society — Wound Irrigation Technique
questions.source_detail: Proper Direction and Technique for Wound Irrigation

questions.stem: A nurse is counseling a parent about the HPV vaccine for their preteen child. The nurse should explain that this vaccine primarily helps prevent:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"No specific health conditions are meaningfully prevented by receiving this vaccine","B":"HPV-related cancers, including cervical cancer, and genital warts","C":"Only unrelated, common childhood illnesses that are unaffected by this particular vaccine","D":"Only minor, self-limited skin infections, with no relationship to any cancer risk"}}
questions.rationale: The HPV vaccine helps prevent infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) strains associated with several cancers, most notably cervical cancer, as well as other HPV-related cancers and genital warts. The CDC recommends routine vaccination starting around ages 11-12.
questions.source_name: CDC — HPV Vaccination Recommendations
questions.source_detail: HPV Vaccine and Cancer Prevention

questions.stem: A nurse is providing health promotion teaching about colorectal cancer screening for an average-risk client. Per current guidelines, screening is generally recommended to begin around what age?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Age 18","B":"Age 80","C":"Age 45","D":"Screening is never recommended for average-risk individuals"}}
questions.rationale: Current guidelines (such as from the American Cancer Society and USPSTF) generally recommend colorectal cancer screening begin around age 45 for average-risk individuals, with the specific screening method and interval individualized based on risk factors and provider discussion.
questions.source_name: American Cancer Society / USPSTF — Colorectal Cancer Screening Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Recommended Screening Start Age for Average-Risk Individuals

questions.stem: A nurse identifies signs of possible intimate partner violence during a client assessment, and the client seems hesitant and unsure where to turn for help. An appropriate resource to offer this client is:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"No meaningful resources at all existing for a client in this kind of situation, so no referral should be offered despite the client's hesitancy","B":"Direct advice for the client to simply leave the relationship immediately, with no further discussion of the client's own safety concerns","C":"Information about the National Domestic Violence Hotline, along with a private, safe conversation about resources and safety planning tailored to the client","D":"Immediate law enforcement involvement arranged without first discussing this with the client, despite their current hesitancy and uncertainty"}}
questions.rationale: When a nurse identifies possible intimate partner violence, an appropriate response includes providing information about resources such as the National Domestic Violence Hotline, along with a private, nonjudgmental conversation about safety planning and options, respecting the client's autonomy and readiness to act.
questions.source_name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — Healthcare Provider Resource Guidance
questions.source_detail: Appropriate Nursing Response and Resource Provision

questions.stem: A client whose spouse died over a year ago continues to experience intense grief that significantly impairs their ability to work, sleep, and maintain relationships, and a family member wonders if this is just taking longer than usual. The nurse should recognize this as potentially consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Postpartum depression, a diagnosis that would not apply to this particular client's situation or the symptoms actually described here","B":"Complicated (prolonged) grief, which may benefit from further evaluation and specialized support given how significantly it is impairing this client's functioning","C":"A sign that the client should be actively discouraged from discussing their loss with anyone, including the concerned family member","D":"A normal, expected grief response requiring no further clinical evaluation, despite the significant functional impairment being described"}}
questions.rationale: While grief is a normal and individualized process without a fixed timeline, persistent, intense grief that significantly impairs daily functioning well beyond typical timeframes may indicate complicated (or prolonged) grief, which can benefit from further evaluation and specialized therapeutic support.
questions.source_name: Center for Complicated Grief — Prolonged Grief Disorder Recognition
questions.source_detail: Distinguishing Complicated Grief from Normal Grief

questions.stem: A nurse intentionally draws on their own communication style, self-awareness, and genuine presence to build trust and support a client's emotional needs during a difficult conversation about a new diagnosis. This concept is known as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Projection, a defense mechanism that does not describe the intentional, self-aware approach being used here","B":"Countertransference, a phenomenon involving the nurse's own unresolved feelings rather than the intentional approach being described","C":"Therapeutic use of self, the intentional and self-aware use of one's own personality and presence to support a client","D":"Professional detachment exclusively, an approach that would actually work against the genuine presence being described here"}}
questions.rationale: "Therapeutic use of self" refers to a nurse's intentional and self-aware use of their own personality, communication style, and genuine presence as a tool to build trust, support, and connection with clients, a foundational concept in psychiatric-mental health nursing and therapeutic relationships broadly.
questions.source_name: Psychiatric-Mental Health Nursing Foundations — Therapeutic Use of Self
questions.source_detail: Definition and Application of Therapeutic Use of Self

questions.stem: A nurse is applying crisis intervention principles with a client in acute distress after a sudden job loss, and a colleague suggests just telling the client exactly what they should do next to fix the situation. After ensuring safety, an appropriate next step is generally to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Making every decision on the client's behalf, without seeking any of their own input, similar to what the colleague just suggested doing","B":"Assess the crisis and help the client identify their own coping resources and support systems, rather than simply directing them as the colleague suggested","C":"Immediately ending the interaction with the client without any further assessment of their current level of distress at all","D":"Deliberately avoiding any discussion of the job loss that actually precipitated this particular crisis for the client right now"}}
questions.rationale: After ensuring immediate safety, crisis intervention generally involves assessing the nature and severity of the crisis, and helping the client identify and mobilize their own coping resources, strengths, and support systems, empowering them to work toward stabilization and problem-solving.
questions.source_name: Crisis Intervention Foundations — Phases of Crisis Intervention
questions.source_detail: Assessment and Resource Identification in Crisis Intervention
